{{DISPLAYTITLE:''p''-variation}} 
In [[mathematical analysis]], '''''p''-variation''' is a collection of [[Norm (mathematics)|seminorm]]s on functions from an ordered set to a [[metric space]], indexed by a real number <math>p\geq 1</math>. ''p''-variation is a measure of the regularity or smoothness of a function. Specifically, if <math>f:I\to(M,d)</math>, where <math>(M,d)</math> is a metric space and ''I'' a totally ordered set, its ''p''-variation is:

<math> \| f \|_{p\text{-var}} = \left(\sup_D\sum_{t_k\in D}d(f(t_k),f(t_{k-1}))^p\right)^{1/p}</math>

where ''D'' ranges over all finite [[partition of an interval|partitions of the interval]] ''I''.

The ''p'' variation of a function decreases with ''p''. If ''f'' has finite ''p''-variation and ''g'' is an ''α''-Hölder [[continuous function]], then <math>g\circ f</math> has finite <math>\frac{p}{\alpha}</math>-variation.

The case when ''p'' is one is called [[total variation]], and functions with a finite 1-variation are called [[bounded variation]] functions.

This concept should not be confused with the notion of p-th variation along a sequence of partitions, which is computed as a limit along a given sequence <math>(D_n)</math> of time partitions:<ref>
{{Cite journal
  | last1 = Cont | first1 = R.
  | last2 = Perkowski | first2 = N.
  | year = 2019
  | title = Pathwise integration and change of variable formulas for continuous paths with arbitrary regularity
  | journal = Transactions of the American Mathematical Society
  | volume = 6
 | pages = 161-186
 | doi = 10.1090/btran/34
  | doi-access = free| arxiv = 1803.09269}}</ref>

<math> [ f ]_{p} = \left(\lim_{n\to\infty} \sum_{t^n_k\in D_n} d(f(t^n_k),f(t^n_{k-1}))^p\right)</math>


For example for p=2, this corresponds to the concept of quadratic variation, which is different from 2-variation.

== Link with Hölder norm ==

One can interpret the ''p''-variation as a parameter-independent version of the Hölder norm, which also extends to discontinuous functions. 

If ''f'' is ''α''&ndash;[[Hölder continuous]] (i.e. its α&ndash;Hölder norm is finite) then its <math>\frac1{\alpha}</math>-variation is finite. Specifically, on an interval [''a'',''b''], <math>\| f \|_{\frac1\alpha\text{-var}}\le \| f \|_{\alpha}(b-a)^\alpha</math>. 

If ''p'' is less than ''q'' then the space of functions of finite ''p''-variation on a compact set is continuously embedded with norm 1 into those of finite ''q''-variation. I.e. 
<math>\|f\|_{q\text{-var}}\le \|f\|_{p\text{-var}}</math>. However unlike the analogous situation with Hölder spaces the embedding is not compact. For example, consider the real functions on [0,1] given by <math>f_n(x)=x^n</math>. They are uniformly bounded in 1-variation and converge pointwise to a discontinuous function ''f'' but this not only is not a convergence in ''p''-variation for any ''p'' but also is not [[uniform convergence]].

== Application to Riemann–Stieltjes integration ==

If ''f'' and ''g'' are functions from [''a'',&nbsp;''b''] to <math>\mathbb{R}</math> with no common discontinuities and with ''f'' having finite ''p''-variation and ''g'' having finite ''q''-variation, with <math>\frac1p+\frac1q>1</math> then the [[Riemann–Stieltjes Integral]]
:<math>\int_a^b f(x) \, dg(x):=\lim_{|D|\to 0}\sum_{t_k\in D}f(t_k)[g(t_{k+1})-g({t_k})]</math>
is well-defined. This integral is known as the ''Young integral'' because it comes from {{harvtxt|Young|1936}}.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://fabricebaudoin.wordpress.com/2012/12/25/lecture-7-youngs-integral/|title = Lecture 7. Young's integral|date = 25 December 2012}}</ref> The value of this definite integral is bounded by the Young-Loève estimate as follows 
:<math>\left|\int_a^b f(x) \, dg(x)-f(\xi)[g(b)-g(a)]\right|\le C\,\|f\|_{p\text{-var}}\|\,g\|_{q\text{-var}}</math>
<!--Why does slide 7 of http://web.sgh.waw.pl/~rlocho/UCT_talk.pdf have an extra factor of 2 on the RHS? Other sources don't? XXXXX -->
where ''C'' is a constant which only depends on ''p'' and ''q'' and ξ is any number between ''a'' and ''b''.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Friz|first1=Peter K.|last2=Victoir|first2=Nicolas|author-link1=Peter Friz|title=Multidimensional Stochastic Processes as Rough Paths: Theory and Applications|date=2010|publisher=Cambridge University Press|edition=Cambridge Studies in Advanced Mathematics}}</ref>
If ''f'' and ''g'' are continuous, the indefinite integral <math>F(w)=\int_a^w f(x) \, dg(x)</math> is a continuous function with finite ''q''-variation: If ''a'' ≤ ''s'' ≤ ''t'' ≤ ''b'' then <math>\|F\|_{q\text{-var};[s,t]}</math>, its ''q''-variation on [''s'',''t''], is bounded by 
<math>C\|g\|_{q\text{-var};[s,t]}(\|f\|_{p\text{-var};[s,t]}+\|f\|_{\infty;[s,t]})\le2C\|g\|_{q\text{-var};[s,t]}(\|f\|_{p\text{-var};[a,b]}+f(a))</math>
where ''C'' is a constant which only depends on ''p'' and ''q''.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Lyons|first1=Terry|last2=Caruana|first2=Michael|last3=Levy|first3=Thierry|title=Differential equations driven by rough paths, vol. 1908 of Lecture Notes in Mathematics|date=2007|publisher=Springer}}</ref>

== Differential equations driven by signals of finite ''p''-variation, ''p'' < 2 ==
A function from <math>\mathbb{R}^{d}</math> to ''e''&nbsp;×&nbsp;''d'' real matrices is called an  <math>\mathbb{R}^{e}</math>-valued one-form on <math>\mathbb{R}^{d}</math>.

If ''f'' is a Lipschitz continuous <math>\mathbb{R}^{e}</math>-valued one-form on <math>\mathbb{R}^{d}</math>, and ''X'' is a continuous function from the interval [''a'',&nbsp;''b''] to <math>\mathbb{R}^{d}</math> with finite ''p''-variation with ''p'' less than 2, then the integral of ''f'' on ''X'', <math>\int_a^b f(X(t))\,dX(t)</math>, can be calculated because each component of ''f''(''X''(''t'')) will be a path of finite ''p''-variation and the integral is a sum of finitely many Young integrals. It provides the solution to the equation <math>dY=f(X)\,dX</math> driven by the path ''X''.

More significantly, if ''f'' is a Lipschitz continuous <math>\mathbb{R}^{e}</math>-valued one-form on <math>\mathbb{R}^{e}</math>, and ''X'' is a continuous function from the interval [''a'',&nbsp;''b''] to <math>\mathbb{R}^{d}</math> with finite ''p''-variation with ''p'' less than 2, then Young integration is enough to establish the solution of the equation <math>dY=f(Y)\,dX</math> driven by the path ''X''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://fabricebaudoin.wordpress.com/2012/12/26/lecture-8-youngs-differential-equations/|title = Lecture 8. Young's differential equations|date = 26 December 2012}}</ref>

== Differential equations driven by signals of finite ''p''-variation, ''p'' ≥ 2 ==
The theory of [[rough path]]s generalises the Young integral and Young differential equations and makes heavy use of the concept of ''p''-variation.

== For Brownian motion ==

''p''-variation should be contrasted with the [[quadratic variation]] which is used in [[stochastic analysis]], which takes one [[stochastic process]] to another. In particular the definition of quadratic variation looks a bit like the definition of ''p''-variation, when ''p'' has the value 2. Quadratic variation is defined as a limit as the partition gets finer, whereas ''p''-variation is a supremum over all partitions. Thus the quadratic variation of a process could be smaller than its 2-variation. If ''W''<sub>''t''</sub> is a standard [[Wiener process|Brownian motion]] on [0,&nbsp;''T''], then with probability one its ''p''-variation is infinite for <math>p\le2</math> and finite otherwise.  The quadratic variation of ''W'' is <math>[W]_T=T</math>.

== Computation of ''p''-variation for discrete time series ==

For a discrete time series of observations ''X<sub>0</sub>,...,X<sub>N</sub>'' it is straightforward to compute its ''p''-variation with complexity of [[Big-O notation|''O'']](''N<sup>2</sup>''). Here is an example C++ code using [[dynamic programming]]:
<syntaxhighlight lang="cpp">
double p_var(const std::vector<double>& X, double p) {
	if (X.size() == 0)
		return 0.0;
	std::vector<double> cum_p_var(X.size(), 0.0);   // cumulative p-variation
	for (size_t n = 1; n < X.size(); n++) {
		for (size_t k = 0; k < n; k++) {
			cum_p_var[n] = std::max(cum_p_var[n], cum_p_var[k] + std::pow(std::abs(X[n] - X[k]), p));
		}
	}
	return std::pow(cum_p_var.back(), 1./p);
}
</syntaxhighlight>
There exist much more efficient, but also more complicated, algorithms for <math>\mathbb{R}</math>-valued processes<ref>
{{Cite journal
  | last1 = Butkus | first1 = V.
  | last2 = Norvaiša | first2 = R.
  | year = 2018
  | title = Computation of p-variation
  | journal = Lithuanian Mathematical Journal
  | volume = 58
 | issue = 4
 | pages = 360–378
 | doi = 10.1007/s10986-018-9414-3
  | s2cid = 126246235
 }}</ref>
<ref name="p-var-github">{{Cite web|url=https://github.com/khumarahn/p-var|title = P-var| website=[[GitHub]] |date = 8 May 2020}}</ref>
and for processes in arbitrary metric spaces.<ref name="p-var-github"/>
